name: 3 - Designing Smarter Engagement with AI
content:
WEBVTT
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: The results of our… Pole?
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: While I say that the request to remain mute is only, in connection with dogs and cats and kids and ringing phones, we very much want to hear from you throughout, and especially at the end, because we're going to leave a lot of time for questions. So please, feel free to use the chat.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: We have a lot of experts in the room, people who are doing interesting things in your own work, and we are very much here to teach and learn from one another. If you have questions or comments, again, preferably to share those in the Q&A,
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: A button you'll find at the bottom, maybe we can write some instructions in the chat about where to find that Q&A. There's so many buttons at the bottom, might be hard to find. But to use the chat or the Q&A to ask questions, and we'll leave plenty of time for conversation as part of this.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Okay, let me share some slides here.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And while I'm doing that, Dane, perhaps you want to quickly introduce yourself, and then we'll go ahead and dive in.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Sure, thank you, Beth. My name is Dane Gambrell, I'm a research fellow, with the GovLab and with Innovate US, where I study collective intelligence and AI, and in particular, how, AI can allow us to
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: to reach communities more accessibly and more efficiently and more effectively with these kinds of public engagement that we will talk about in the workshop today. So thank you for the opportunity to participate.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Fantastic. Dane has an absolutely encyclopedic knowledge of engagement happening all over the world, what works and what doesn't work, and so I'm delighted that he can join me for this today. So many of you may have heard about the Irish Citizens Assembly, probably one of the most successful, in many ways, instances of democratic participation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Where a representative sample of 99 members of the Irish public have come together to deliberate.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: leading to changes in Irish law around abortion, for example, or same-sex marriage. It's what led to Ireland's make… creating the first referendum, successful referendum, on same-sex marriage. But even this extraordinarily successful example of engagement has only happened 6 times
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: In 15 years.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: In Singapore, they similarly adopted a kind of citizen-jury, citizen assembly model, tried it four times, and then stopped.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: That is a very, very common problem. Citizen engagement, despite having fantastic technology, even before AI, we've had, you know, 30 years of the World Wide Web allowing us to do new forms of engagement, and yet citizen engagement too often remains tokenistic, it remains occasional, or it remains very small.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So part of what we're here to do today, our goal for this whole series, is to try to accelerate
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: improve and institutionalize what we do by way of citizen engagement. The argument underlying the series that we're running here, together with the Allen Lab for Democratic Renovation, Danielle Allen and her team from Harvard, and we're very grateful for their participation, we are taking turns on running these sessions, is to really figure out, as Danielle talked about in our
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: first session, ways that we can connect participation To decision-making and to action.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So, the conversation we're going to have today is really rooted in some work that Dane and I did a few years ago together with Nesta.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Nesta, as many of you know, is the innovation lab of the UK, and together with Nesta, we looked at 30 global case studies of successful forms of citizen engagement and participation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Where that engagement was connected to impact, it wasn't just people talking, it was actually institutions listening.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And it was forms of engagement that have been adopted repeated over time.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So what we're interested in is what works. And that's what led us to developing, to essentially reverse engineering this checklist of 9 questions.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: That every innovator that we spoke to, that every public engagement professional that we spoke to, said were really the ingredients, questions they had to be able to answer in order to run a successful engagement.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: We're here to explore not just what those factors are, but how AI can help us accelerate what we do in connection with that work.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Now, to be very clear at the outset, we are not talking here about getting faster by replacing engagement with AI. We are not talking about saying, look, you can just go ask ChatGPT instead of asking
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: communities. We assume, as we've talked about in our other sessions, that we're all in agreement about the need to do engagement and why it's valuable. So we won't spend a lot of time rehashing that argument. Rather, we're going to get into more nitty-gritty today of really trying to look at these nine factors.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: The slides are shared, everything we talk about here is shared, and we will put it up online, so no need to take any notes.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: But as we're going along, if you've had experience, if you agree with these questions, disagree, have figured out good ways of using AI to answer these questions, we'd love for you to share your experience in the chat.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Okay, let me pause there, and I'm gonna dive in.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And all good? Just checking that everybody can hear and see.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Fantastic. Okay, step one.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: This may seem fairly obvious, but I have seen, in my experience, more often than not.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: people going out and doing engagement because they have to, not because they need to. That is to say, there is some sense that we have to go out and do stakeholder consultation, we have to go out and be seen listening to the public.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: But we're not really clear why… what we're asking and why we're asking it.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So it is extraordinarily important to define what the purpose is for that engagement, and to ensure that everybody is on the same page about that shared purpose.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Again, that may be easier said than done. It sounds obvious in principle, but in practice, it can be quite hard.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: When we ran our task force on AI for the state of New Jersey, we wanted to go out and make… we needed to go out and make policy for what we would do as the state around AI, to protect workers, to protect the environment, to upskill our residents and our students.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: But to do that, and really make those policies effectively in a way that was responding to what citizen need was, what we wanted to do was to go out and understand what the problems were that people were facing.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So in order to formulate our questions, in order to even go out and ask people.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: what they thought the questions were. We had to get agreement on what the question was that we needed to ask. And again, I'm going to breeze through a lot of these examples, so if anything is unclear about how we did it, the mechanics.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: please feel free to put notes in the chat or to ask afterwards. So we used an open-source AI tool that was free called All Our Ideas.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: developed by Princeton and Citizens Foundation, to go out and ask people, and we used AI really to help us formulate that question.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: You'll see on the screen there just a very short question, but what we did to drive the entire engagement, what we did with the public, what we did with public servants as we went out and talked to stakeholders, what we… was we used AI to really help us write a compelling goal statement for why we are doing this engagement.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And again, I think it's an extraordinarily helpful use of AI that can give us an opportunity to define our goals up front, to ensure that we're aligned on what it is we need to know from people so we can understand what success is.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: If I'm going to go out and do that, and to really make sure that everybody is on the same page, that is to say, our internal team, the public itself, about why we're asking, all of our stakeholders are clear on what we want to do, we also have to figure out
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: who it is we need to go ask. And that is not always an easy question.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: We know that hearing from diverse voices can actually help us to make better policy. When we can go out and ask people, and by this, I mean both people with lived experiences and people with what I'll call credentialed or academic expertise.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: When I can hear from both of those types of experts.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: I'm going to get useful know-how that can help me better understand both what the problem is and what the solutions are of what I might want to develop.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So, I develop a targeted outreach plan. Before AI, maybe I have an office of public engagement or stakeholder engagement that says, these are the usual suspects you need to go ask.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: But with AI, I can help uncover and map other people I might want to engage with. So, for example, during COVID, we partnered… the state of New Jersey partnered with the Federation of American Scientists to create a network of 600 PhD-credentialed scientists
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: to help us crowdsource answers to people's COVID questions.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: That was a very, very hard job to go out and find those 600 people to participate and to get them engaged. Now, with AI, I can do such a better job of actually identifying who those people are, and speed up that process of outreach.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: In Brazil, the Senate of Brazil invites citizens to participate in every legislative hearing by writing questions
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: That they want, senators to ask of testifying witnesses.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: How do they do that? They look at…
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: who's participated before, but more importantly, I think, they look at what people's profession is. So if you're registered as a doctor or a nurse, and there's a hearing about a healthcare issue.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: They're going to reach out to you and say, hey, do you have anything that you want to ask? So this ability, again, to use AI to map and identify who it is I might want to ask.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Whether expert or public, and then to go out and reach those people gives me an opportunity to find the right people.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: I'm gonna skip ahead over, this is just another example here.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: But I want to skip to this example, which I think is an even more compelling one. This is a project that Dane and I are both involved in, together with colleagues, where we are building an AI tool
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Together with parents and teachers and educators, that helps to summarize and translate a child's individualized education plan, the plan you get when your child has a disability in public school.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Again, we are engaging with diverse voices, not just with PhD educators, but with families of kids with disabilities in building this tool. So all that to say, as we're thinking about, as we're thinking about both
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: whom to reach out to, how to reach out to them, and what to reach out to them about, I think there are opportunities here to think about using AI to help us to do that. Let me stop the share here and pass the slides to Dane, who's going to take us forward with our next couple of factors.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Great, thanks, Beth. Just give me a second, and I will pull up, the slides where you left off, and screen share that.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And in the meantime, if people have comments, questions, your own experience, please share things in the chat, and…
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: We'll keep going.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Okay, great. I'm assuming everyone can see, my slides just fine.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Okay, great, thanks. So naturally, once you've figured out who are the right communities and the right types of people that you're trying to reach, as Beth described, the next step is to think through how you're going to go out and reach those people.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So this is really about thinking through, the strategies that you're using to reach people, and making sure that those strategies are targeted to the interests and the priorities of the communities that you want to hear from.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So that's also about making outreach accessible, not just accessible in terms of technical accessibility, although that's part of this, but also accessibility in terms of the language that you're using, the format, the channel, whether that's in person or through, online outreach through social media, through mailing lists, and that you're really reaching people where they are.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And why this is so important is that without, really targeted outreach and targeted outreach to diverse communities who are underrepresented in the existing decision-making processes, we risk just hearing from the people whose perspectives are already represented, in the decisions that we're making, and then we risk reaching out on learning from perspectives from other people that are
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Just as, if not more valuable.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So one of the really exciting things here is that AI can help us to accelerate that outreach process, to do it faster, and to amplify the amount of outreach that we can do. So I'll talk in the next slide about an example of how an AI-powered chatbot can be a good way of doing this.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: But there's also ways to use
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: you know, easily accessible through AI tools like ChatGBT, Claude, Gemini, to create multiple versions of outreach materials that can be tailored to different audiences.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And to help with translating those materials into multiple languages, with simplifying technical jargon, to make sure that the language that you're using to advertise the opportunity to participate is as plain and as accessible as possible.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So I'll show an example here. So the city of Bogota, Colombia, has deployed an AI-powered WhatsApp chatbot that they call Chatico, to improve civic participation and how they deliver services to residents. So the platform is AI capabilities built in that allow it to understand and to process natural language, to answer people's questions, and to guide residents through engagement processes.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: processes.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So to take an example, the city used this tool last year as part of its participatory budgeting campaign, where people proposed ideas and then voted on projects they want to see implemented in their neighborhoods.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: In just under 2 weeks, the campaign collected over 130,000 votes from more than 50,000 residents, who weighed in on over 2,700 budget proposals. And so that made it the largest digital participatory budgeting process ever recorded in Bogota, with this chatbot handling nearly 90% of those digital votes.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So this example is notable not just for the scale, but for who participated. So, 57% of people who voted in this process were women. There was also strong representation from migrants and from people with disabilities, and these are all groups that are often excluded from civic processes.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And so why this worked is that the platform's design,
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: really prioritizes plain language, mobile-first design being a WhatsApp chatbot, and it's designed in a way that it guides users through the workflow of how to participate in the participatory budgeting process and why it matters. And all of those design factors help to reduce barriers to participation and make it more accessible and more impactful.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So the next step in our guide is thinking through who is the right owner for your participatory process.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So why this is important is that we know that, these kinds of projects, you're usually not doing them alone. They're usually delivered by coalitions, by groups of partners, so this part of the checklist is really making sure to think through who's responsible for what components of the project.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And especially making sure to assign responsibility for making use of the community's input.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And then, with AI in the mix,
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: another part of this is really thinking through, you know, the tough decisions that project owners have to make about what types of tasks AI is and isn't suitable for, and then when it is used, making sure that it's used in a way that's ethical and that's responsible.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And as Beth described at the beginning, also, responsible use is making sure that AI is, on tap, not on top, that it's not being seen as a replacement, either for human decision making, or for real engagement with communities.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: One example of how generative AI could be helpful here is by, helping to think through, like, what those roles and responsibilities should be, helping, for example, to write up descriptions of those roles, but understanding that it's really, you know, you and your partners that are responsible for making the determination of who should be responsible for what.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So the example that I'll give here is a project that's ongoing from the state of California, where the state is working together with communities impacted by the Los Angeles wildfires to collaboratively design an action plan for rebuilding.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So during its first phase, communities deliberated online about what the state's priorities should be when it comes to, recovery and rebuilding. And they collected more than 1,300 comments using a deliberation platform called Othello, that uses AI to help with analyzing, with synthesizing large amounts of public input.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: The reason, though, that I give this example here is around the partnership. So the state's government operations agency and California's Office of Data and Innovation, together with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, are leading the development of this program.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: They're also partnering with the City and County of the City of Los Angeles and the County of Los Angeles, I should say, together with community organizations to make sure that the initiative can reach community members.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And so the reason we give this example here is that this is an initiative that's owned within state government. It's been championed by California's governor, Gavin Newsom, and while this is an ongoing process, we don't know yet what the outcomes will be. Having responsible owners within the state government
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Makes it much more likely that the community's priorities will translate into implementable programs and, and policies.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Okay, so then, step 5 of our checklist is, thinking through what the incentives for participation should be.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So, how do we make sure that people know why they should participate?
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So, those incentives could be extrinsic motivators. So, for example, people who, you know, suggest an idea get entered into a drawing to win a prize, or they might be given a stipend in exchange for their time, or they could be intrinsic motivators. So, you know, just appeals to people's desire to do good and to fulfill their civic duties.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Incentives are also about reducing barriers to participation, so particularly if we're talking about something that's, an in-person,
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: engagement, offering, you know, support, like child care, like elder care, like, support with transportation, transportation vouchers, what are sometimes called wraparound services, can help to reduce some of those barriers. And so this is a practical consideration, but it's also, you know, about, showing respect for the time, the expertise, and the experience that people are contributing.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: When it comes to AI, you know.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: AI can be useful here in a bunch of different ways. I'll give an example in the next slide about how real-time summaries and visualizations can serve as motivators. But even something as simple as using AI to create personalized thank-you notes or personalized certificates of participation that help people feel like their contributions are valued is something that can be,
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Be… be helpful.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So the example that I'll give here is from, a community in, Londonderry, Derry, Northern Ireland.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So each year, the Voice Matters Initiative, convenes a people's panel, basically a citizen's assembly, where residents of Derry Northern Ireland talk together about what their community's future should look like.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And so, some of the deliberations in past years have explored mental health in the area and how it could be improved, or how to create a better future for young people.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: What's really interesting is this year they've started experimenting, with a platform called Echo, developed by the Belgian… or, developed by the company, Dembrain,
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Which uses, AI to transcribe the conversation, to identify common themes, and to create visualizations based on participants' ideas in real time.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And so why… this is really transformative, because in contrast to past years where these deliberations would happen, and then facilitators would have to get together over this series of several weekends and compare notes and pull findings from the deliberations manually, now the AI transcription and summarization allows them to pull those insights in real time, and to report them back
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: to the participants at the end of each deliberation, and also to create visualizations of participants' ideas, like you see, on the slide here. And so that's…
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Really, an incentive because it helps people to understand that their voices are being heard and that they're being valued.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: In addition, you know, Voice Matters also provides some of those financial support, so participants receive a stipend for their time, and the initiative also covers related costs like childcare.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So this, together, this helps people see that their voices matter, reduces barriers, and helps to see why, participating is a good and impactful use of their time.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Okay, so then the last piece of the checklist that I'll talk about before handing it back to Beth is step number 6.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Have you defined the tasks?
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So step 6 is really about thinking through what you're asking participants to contribute, and then how you're providing instructions, and making sure that those instructions are clear, and that they're matched to participants' abilities and their expertise.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So why this is especially important in an AI-enabled engagement is, if you're gonna bring AI into the mix, it's important to kind of think through, you know, how you're going to use AI.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: whether that's summarizing or clustering, categorizing, and then to make sure that you're collecting responses in a way that allows you to then do that AI-enabled analysis later.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And then,
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Thinking about, you know, generative AI tools, something like ChatGPT, Claude, etc. can be really helpful in just helping to define and refine instructions to make tasks clearer and accessible and easier to follow.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: It also can help you to collect input in new ways. So, whereas some people might be really comfortable writing up a written description of their idea, or of their comment or their opinion, other people might be more comfortable, you know, talking through their idea out loud. And these transcription or speech-to-text, capabilities can allow those people to be able to give their input that way.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So the example that I'll give here is from Bowling Green, Kentucky. So in this case, local leaders from Warren County, Kentucky, invited residents of Bowling Green to share their vision for their community's future, as part of their long-term planning process. So they had a really simple and clearly defined task, which is they asked people to respond to an open-ended prompt that simply asked.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: What do you want to see your community's future look like over the next 25 years?
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And then in this online participation platform, participants were shown each other's submissions. They could either agree or disagree with other suggestions.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And so, where AI comes in is AI really allowed this initiative to work at scale. So nearly 8,000 participants submitted nearly 4,000 ideas, more than a million votes over the course of a month.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: A level of participation that would not be feasible in an in-person deliberation.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And they used, the Polis platform to facilitate the deliberation. They also used Google Jigsaw's sense-making tool to categorize the ideas, to identify areas of agreement and disagreement, and to summarize the overall findings into a really, nifty, interactive report, one, one slide of which you see here.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: And so why we give this example is by, by really clearly defining those tasks for input, the organizers enabled both scale and depth.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: So participants knew exactly what was expected of them, how they were meant to give input, and then also how those AI tools were going to synthesize the contributions. And so that allowed, the organizers to collect a huge amount of input.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Without losing the original meaning of people's ideas.
 
 Dane Gambrell, The GovLab: Okay, and with that, I'll hand it back to you, Beth, to talk us through the rest of the checklist.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Fantastic. If you want to keep, going with your slides, I think that would be great. Let me pause for a moment to say, two things. One is, there's a lot of great questions coming in in the chat. Please keep them coming. We're going to wrap up shortly and give you a chance to ask your questions. We'll do some combination of
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: essentially call… we'll call on you if you've already asked a question, and we'll also invite you to raise your hand. Secondly, some of the things that Dane has talked about,
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: All of these platforms are profiled, by People Powered, who spoke for us last time, and who have a great resource just on platforms, and which thing does which. But again, we'll share all the information that we've talked about here previously. And the Bowling Green project that you just mentioned, Dane, they are coming up in our series, and we'll get to hear from Bowling Green, the City of Bowling Green.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And their tech providers about how they did what they did.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Okay, so let's come back here, and I just want to remind everybody that AI here is just the tool. I want to just refresh that we're arguing that these are the key questions you need to answer.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: And AI is just a tool in the toolkit to help you potentially answer these questions faster and easier, to allow us to do more engagement.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: So the last three things, we need to do, and you can keep going here, is to really figure out, essentially, do I have a plan? Do I have clear steps? You know, do… have I project managed this thing? Have I worked backwards from the end to figure out what I need to do with each step?
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: But more importantly, not just at each step of one engagement, have I thought through the whole policy-making process. So one of the things we tend to do now, because engagement is so difficult, is to only do engagement once.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: We do it at one snapshot or one point in the process of making a policy or designing a service. Part of our argument here is that what we can do is to think about how to use engagement, whether it's with members of the public, whether it's with credentialed experts.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: whether it's with a subset of stakeholders, that there's engagement we can do at every stage of the policy-making process. So that can include defining the problem, coming up with solutions, implementing those solutions, or really evaluating what we've done. So we want to think about both
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: the workflow in terms of the whole policy-making process, and then the process of running the engagement. We can keep going here.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Ai can obviously help us with any of that kind of, project management task. As Dane already pointed out, so I won't belabor it, and by the way, we're going to hear much more about this from the City of Hamburg, which is coming up, talking about their project.
 
 Beth S. Noveck, InnovateUS/The GovLab/NJ: Gen AI can really help to shrink how long it takes us to do many of these phases. So when I can rapidly summarize and draw insights from one phase.
 
 Beth S. Novec
 
 [... truncated ...]
